pages.title: Full Stack and Infrastructure Engineer Interview Preparation

blocks.text: Prepared for Muhammad Awais | Role in Al Rawdah, Abu Dhabi, UAE

Your main interview message: you can connect backend engineering, Azure deployment, and production operations for an AI platform. This guide contains 48 questions with sample answers, system design and troubleshooting drills, practical exercises, and a seven-day preparation plan.

Practice answers aloud for 60 to 90 seconds, then expand only when asked. Personalize every project story with details you can defend. Experience answers draw on your CV; design answers describe what you would do. Cost governance is a preparation priority because the CV does not establish ownership of budgets or quantified savings.
1 Tell me about yourself

I am a Senior Full Stack Engineer with more than eight years of experience delivering enterprise applications and cloud platforms. My backend work includes ASP.NET Core, Node.js and TypeScript, and Python FastAPI. At USS IT Consultants, contracted to 7X/EPG, my work includes AI-enabled services, a production RAG pipeline, infrastructure automation, and operational support. Previously, I worked on logistics at GAC, Azure transformation at Merik, and airline systems at Calrom. This role interests me because it combines backend delivery with the deployment, observability, and reliability responsibilities I have handled in production.
2 Why are you a good fit for this role

The role needs someone who can build APIs and keep the platform dependable after release. My CV includes AKS and Azure Container Apps, Terraform and Bicep, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions, and incident response using Azure Monitor and Application Insights. I also understand the application side of AI through Azure OpenAI, retrieval, and Python inference services. I would use that combination to help AI and frontend engineers deliver features with deployment controls, measurable service health, and clear operational ownership.
3 What would you prioritize in the first month

First, I would map the services, dependencies, production access, current costs, and incident history. I would verify that a failed release can be reversed and that backups can actually be restored. Next, I would agree on service objectives and identify gaps in alerts, secret handling, and infrastructure automation. By the end of the month, I would aim to deliver one measurable improvement, such as a safer release path or an actionable dashboard, while documenting a prioritized reliability and cost backlog.
4 How should you handle an unfamiliar technology

I would state my exposure accurately, connect it to a relevant concept I know, and describe how I would validate a solution. For example: I have production experience with Azure infrastructure and monitoring, but my CV does not document ownership of cloud budgets. I can explain a cost-control design and would validate it with the billing owner before applying production spending controls. This is stronger than claiming a project outcome I cannot substantiate.
Use Situation, Task, Action, Result. Be specific about your contribution and what the team delivered. Bring a simple architecture sketch for your two strongest projects.
5 Describe your AI platform work

At 7X/EPG, the platform combined content services, event processing, and ML inference. My CV describes a backend using .NET services, Node.js NestJS on Azure Functions, and Python FastAPI, with Azure Container Apps and Kubernetes deployment. The retrieval flow used Azure OpenAI, LangChain or Semantic Kernel, Azure AI Search, and pgvector. I would explain my own component ownership, how a request moved through the services, and how we monitored failures. The documented retrieval result was sub-two-second responses; I would clarify the measurement conditions rather than present that as an unconditional SLA.
Prepare follow-ups: Why these three languages? Which service did you own? What was the slowest dependency? How were prompts and retrieval evaluated?
6 Tell me about an infrastructure improvement

My current-role CV records infrastructure provisioning with Terraform and Azure DevOps, including AI service dependencies, in under five minutes. I would frame the problem as repeatable environment creation, explain how modules and environment configuration were organized, and describe validation before deployment. The result I can cite is faster provisioning. I would be ready to define which resources and pipeline stages the five-minute figure includes and separate that timing from application startup, data migration, or manual approval time.
7 Describe a reliability improvement

At GAC, my responsibilities included investigating API, container, messaging, and deployment incidents, executing rollback or recovery, and improving runbooks and alerts after RCA. For the interview, I would choose one real incident and state its symptom, impact, and my action. I would explain how I identified the failing dependency, restored service, and changed the system afterward. My CV supports this responsibility, but it does not give a specific outage timeline, so I would supply only details I remember accurately.
8 Explain the metrics on your CV

The CV records 200K+ daily events, 99.99% message delivery reliability, and 90%+ automated test coverage in the current platform. These measure different things. Event count describes throughput volume; message reliability needs a defined denominator, time window, and treatment of retries; coverage measures exercised code and does not prove correctness. I would explain where the measurements came from and my contribution. I would not relabel message reliability as API availability or claim that the coverage percentage guarantees the system has no defects.

Before the interview, record: exact service owned, workload size, measurement window, dashboard or test report, one failure mode, one tradeoff, and what you would change today. Confirm certificate status and employer dates before repeating them.
9 How would you design an Azure AI agents platform

I would first clarify tenant isolation, request volume, response time, data sensitivity, and whether work is interactive or asynchronous. A starting design is an authenticated API behind API Management, an orchestrator, and queue-backed workers for longer tasks. State belongs in a durable database, documents in storage, and retrieval in a search or vector service. I would use Azure OpenAI for model calls, workload identities for resource access, and tracing across the API, agent run, and tools. I would start with the simplest orchestration that meets the workflow and add services only when there is a clear operational reason.
10 When would you choose AKS or Container Apps

I would choose Container Apps when managed container hosting and scaling satisfy the workload and we want to reduce cluster operations. I would choose AKS when we need Kubernetes-level control, specialized scheduling, operators, or detailed networking and platform extensions. The decision includes team capability, workload behavior, security requirements, and total operating cost. My CV includes both environments. I would compare a representative workload and its operational requirements instead of assuming Kubernetes is always the right answer.
11 How do you separate development test and production

I would use deliberate environment boundaries for identity, configuration, data, deployment permissions, and resource ownership. Production would have restricted access and controlled release paths. Reusable infrastructure modules would keep environments consistent while parameter files hold environment differences. Nonproduction would use synthetic or appropriately sanitized data. I would separate production from nonproduction subscriptions when governance requires it, and verify that service identities cannot cross the boundary. Naming, tags, ownership, and cost reporting would be applied consistently.
12 How would you design availability and recovery

I would agree on a service-level objective, recovery time objective, and recovery point objective before adding redundancy. I would remove single points of failure within the chosen region, use appropriate database backup and replication, and ensure retries and timeouts prevent dependency failures from cascading. If regional recovery is required, I would design the data and identity failover as well as compute. I would test restoration and failover, because replicas and backup configuration alone do not demonstrate recovery. The final design depends on acceptable downtime, data loss, and budget.
Follow-ups: How do private endpoints resolve DNS? How do you rotate credentials? Which dependency limits scaling? Explain that availability zones and a second region solve different failure cases.
13 How would you design an API for agent runs

I would expose a create-run endpoint, a run-status endpoint, and cancellation where the workflow supports it. A long-running request would return HTTP 202 with a run identifier and status location. The API would validate input, authorize the tenant and resource, and persist accepted work before dispatch. Clients could poll or receive streamed progress. I would define versioned request and response contracts, consistent errors, request limits, and a correlation identifier. The API should distinguish accepted, running, succeeded, failed, and canceled states.
14 How do you make a retry safe

For an operation that can create side effects, I would accept an idempotency key scoped to the tenant and operation. I would atomically store the key with a request hash and operation state under a uniqueness constraint. A repeated matching request returns the same run or result; a conflicting payload returns a defined error. I would decide key expiration and behavior for in-progress or failed operations. Retry logic alone is insufficient because a timeout may happen after the original action has already succeeded.
15 What differs between Python async and Node.js concurrency

Both can handle many I/O waits efficiently, but asynchronous syntax does not make blocking work disappear. In Python, I would use nonblocking clients in an async endpoint and move CPU-heavy work to a suitable process or worker service. In Node.js, I would avoid blocking the event loop and use worker threads or separate workers for CPU-heavy tasks. In either stack, I would limit connection pools and concurrency, set deadlines, and measure queueing. Adding unlimited concurrency can overwhelm databases or model quotas.
16 How do you keep events and database state consistent

I would use a transactional outbox when a database update must reliably lead to an event. The transaction writes the business record and an outbox record together. A dispatcher publishes pending records and records progress; consumers deduplicate because publication or delivery can repeat. I would monitor oldest unpublished age, retries, and dead letters. For a multistep business workflow, I would define compensating actions where possible. I would avoid promising end-to-end exactly-once side effects without explaining the boundaries and deduplication mechanism.
Also rehearse: cursor pagination, schema validation, API versioning, authentication versus authorization, database indexes, connection pool exhaustion, and HTTP 401, 403, 409, 429, 502, 503, and 504.

pages.title: CI CD and Infrastructure as Code

blocks.text: 17 Describe a production delivery pipeline

I would run linting, unit and integration tests, dependency and container scanning, then build one immutable artifact and publish it to the registry. Infrastructure changes would have a reviewed plan or preview. The same application artifact would progress through test and production, with environment configuration injected separately. Before rollout, I would check migration compatibility and readiness. After rollout, I would verify errors, latency, and key business behavior. Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions are both represented in my CV; I would explain the actual pipeline I worked on rather than only name the tooling.
18 How would you make deployments reversible

I would retain the previous application version and define the health signals that stop a rollout. A small initial deployment would expand only after its health is acceptable. Recovery could switch traffic back or deploy a known-good image. I would treat database changes separately, using compatible schema expansion before removing old fields later. Some data mutations require a forward fix or restoration rather than a simple application rollback. I would test recovery steps and make ownership clear before production release. [S1]
19 When would you use Terraform or Bicep

Bicep is attractive for Azure-focused resource definitions and integration with Azure Resource Manager. Terraform is useful when a common workflow spans Azure and other providers. For Terraform, I would protect remote state, use backend-supported locking, restrict access, and review plans. For Bicep, I would review what-if output and understand its limitations. For either, I would pin dependencies appropriately, structure reusable modules, and manage secrets outside ordinary configuration files. My CV includes Terraform and Bicep, so I would discuss a real example of each.
20 How do you handle infrastructure drift

I would detect drift through scheduled comparison and investigate why it occurred before changing production. An emergency manual change should be recorded, reviewed, and represented in code if it must remain. If drift should be removed, I would assess impact and apply a controlled correction. I would also check deployment access, ownership, and policy to reduce recurrence. Blindly applying infrastructure code can remove a critical emergency fix; permanently accepting unmanaged drift undermines reproducibility.

Follow-ups: immutable image tags versus digests; secret-free pipeline identity; required reviews; artifact promotion; smoke tests; database expand-and-contract; emergency change reconciliation. Reference: Bicep what-if [S2].
21 What makes a production container image good

I would use a trusted minimal base, build in stages, install only runtime dependencies, and run as a non-root user where supported. The image should not contain credentials or environment-specific settings. I would scan it, record its origin, and deploy an immutable digest. The process should handle termination signals, stop accepting new work, and finish or safely checkpoint current work. I would also check the actual memory profile and writable filesystem needs before enforcing runtime restrictions.
22 Explain readiness liveness and startup probes

Readiness determines whether a pod should receive traffic. Liveness detects a condition that justifies restarting the container. A startup probe protects a slow-starting application before readiness and liveness checks proceed. I would make liveness conservative; a database outage should not cause every healthy application process to restart. Readiness should reflect whether the service can perform its intended work. Probe thresholds and intervals need to match observed startup and failure behavior. [S3]
23 How would you scale workers and APIs

For interactive APIs, I would consider request concurrency, CPU or memory, and latency. For workers, queue depth and the age of the oldest item are often better indicators. Pod scaling and node scaling solve different capacity problems. I would set resource requests and limits based on measurements, define minimum and maximum capacity, and validate that the database and model endpoint can handle the resulting concurrency. More workers can increase throttling and cost if the downstream dependency is already saturated.
24 A pod is failing how do you investigate

I would inspect status, events, current and previous logs, and the last deployment change. Pending can indicate scheduling, capacity, or volume issues. ImagePullBackOff points toward registry access or image references. CrashLoopBackOff means I need the crash cause, such as startup errors, configuration, or failed liveness. OOMKilled suggests examining memory limits and actual allocation. I would restore service with a safe mitigation and then address the cause. I would not increase limits or restart pods repeatedly without understanding the failure.
Practice: kubectl get pods; kubectl describe pod <pod>; kubectl logs <pod> --previous; kubectl get events; kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>
Follow-ups: disruption budgets, availability-zone placement, rolling-update surge, graceful shutdown, resource limits, service discovery, and why an HPA cannot overcome a model quota.
25 What would you monitor on this platform

I would monitor the user journey and its dependencies: run completion and failure rates, p95 and p99 latency, queue age, tool failures, database saturation, and model throttling. For AI workloads, I would add tokens and estimated cost per completed task, repeated tool calls, and evaluation results. Traces would connect API requests to run IDs, model calls, and tool operations, with sensitive content excluded from default logs. My CV includes Azure Monitor, Application Insights, OpenTelemetry, Grafana, Prometheus, and Loki.
26 What are an SLI SLO and error budget

An SLI is the measured indicator, such as the proportion of valid requests completed successfully. An SLO is its target over a specified period. The error budget is the allowed unreliability implied by that target. For example, a 99.9% request-success target permits 0.1% unsuccessful eligible requests; we must define eligibility and measurement. I would use budget consumption to guide release risk and reliability work. I would distinguish an internal objective from a contractual SLA and avoid adopting a target without business agreement.
27 How do you respond to a severe production incident

I would confirm user impact, establish ownership and a communication channel, and capture the incident start time. I would inspect recent changes and current signals, then choose the safest mitigation, such as stopping a rollout or disabling a failing feature. I would keep investigation and restoration coordinated, verify recovery from user-facing signals, and communicate what remains affected. Afterward, I would preserve the timeline, determine contributing causes, and assign prevention work. My documented on-call experience includes rollback, traffic mitigation, and RCA.
28 How do you reduce noisy alerts

I would review whether each alert identifies an actionable user impact or an imminent risk with a known response. I would use appropriate duration windows, group duplicates, route alerts to owners, and attach runbooks. A temporary CPU spike should not automatically page the team if the service remains healthy. I would also detect missing telemetry so silence is not mistaken for health. After incidents, I would review false positives and missed detections, then adjust signals and thresholds based on evidence.
Rehearse an incident update: affected users and functions, current mitigation, next investigation step, and next update time. Do not present an unverified suspected cause as a confirmed root cause.
Use proposed-action language for these answers unless you can add a verified personal example. Do not invent a savings percentage, budget size, or finance responsibility.
29 How would you manage Azure spending

I would establish a spending baseline by environment, service, and owner, then identify major cost drivers and unused resources. I would configure actual and forecast budget alerts at suitable scopes and assign response owners. Azure budgets notify; they do not automatically stop resources, and billing data is delayed, so they cannot serve as an immediate spending cutoff. I would use runtime quotas and an application usage ledger for fast controls, with billing reconciliation afterward. Any automatic restriction of production would need agreed service behavior. [S4]
30 How would you reduce LLM cost without losing quality

I would measure cost per successfully completed task, not only cost per call. Then I would test shorter retrieved context, appropriate output limits, reduced unnecessary retries, and routing simpler tasks to an adequate model. I would consider caching only where tenant permissions and freshness allow it. Agent step limits and tool-call limits prevent runaway loops. Each change needs a representative evaluation set and latency measurements, because a cheaper call can cause more failures, retries, or escalations. I would use current deployment pricing when estimating impact.
31 Explain a token cost calculation

For token-billed calls: cost = input_tokens / 1,000,000 x input_rate + output_tokens / 1,000,000 x output_rate. Hypothetical practice rates of USD 2 per million input tokens and USD 8 per million output tokens give USD 0.012 for 2,000 input and 1,000 output tokens. At 10,000 such calls, that is USD 120. These are invented exercise rates, not a model price quote. A full task estimate also includes extra model calls, embeddings, search, compute, storage, telemetry, and retries; some deployment types use different billing models.
32 How would you investigate a sudden cost spike

I would compare cost and usage by time, deployment, tenant, and workload. I would check recent releases, prompt growth, model-routing changes, traffic volume, repeated tool calls, retries, background jobs, and possible credential misuse. I would contain the driver using targeted limits or a feature switch while preserving critical service. Then I would validate the effect in runtime usage metrics and reconcile billing later. For infrastructure, I would also inspect excess replicas, idle capacity, telemetry ingestion, and unexpected data transfer.

Pragmatic tradeoffs: right-size before commitments; schedule nonproduction shutdown only where safe; reduce log retention by need; set tenant limits; distinguish forecast alerts from immediate enforcement. Prioritize this page in rehearsal.
33 How would you manage secrets and identities

I would prefer workload identities over embedded credentials and grant only the required resource permissions. For AKS, workload identity can federate the Kubernetes service account with an Azure identity. Secrets that remain necessary would be stored in Key Vault with restricted access, rotation, and an audit trail. Pipeline access would use federation where supported. I would ensure local developer access, production runtime access, and deployment access have different scopes. My CV documents Key Vault and Azure AD use; I would describe workload federation as a design approach unless I can verify personal implementation. [S5]
34 How do you isolate tenants

I would derive tenant context from authenticated claims and enforce authorization in each data access path. A client-supplied tenant ID is not sufficient proof of access. Tenant identity must carry through API requests, queued jobs, caches, retrieval filters, and tool calls. I would choose shared or separate databases and compute based on isolation requirements, operational cost, and noisy-neighbor risk. I would test cross-tenant access attempts and avoid caching sensitive results under keys that omit the security context.
35 How would you secure agent tools

I would treat model-generated tool arguments as untrusted input. Each tool would have a narrow contract, validated arguments, independent authorization, and restricted network and data access. Retrieved text would not be allowed to override application permissions. Sensitive actions would have an approval or other explicit authorization boundary and a useful audit record. I would limit steps and external destinations, redact sensitive logs, and test malicious documents. Prompt instructions help guide behavior, but enforcement belongs in application and infrastructure controls.
36 What does DevSecOps mean in your delivery process

I would integrate security checks into ordinary delivery: secret detection, dependency and image scanning, infrastructure review, least-privilege deployment access, and tracked remediation. Critical findings need an agreed release policy and a time-bound exception process where necessary. Runtime controls remain important because a clean scan does not guarantee secure behavior. At GAC, my CV includes automated security scanning and container image signing. I would be ready to explain the actual checks, what happened on failure, and who reviewed exceptions.

Follow-ups: authentication versus authorization; Azure RBAC versus Kubernetes RBAC; private endpoint DNS; certificate rotation; audit logging without exposing prompts or credentials; containment and rotation after a leaked credential.
37 Explain RAG and how you would operate it

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant information and includes it in the model context. I would explain ingestion, parsing, chunking, indexing, permission filtering, retrieval, and generation separately. Operational checks include freshness, retrieval failures, index updates, and latency at each stage. Evaluation should measure whether the right evidence was retrieved and whether the answer is supported, not only whether it sounds fluent. My current-role CV includes Azure AI Search and pgvector with Azure OpenAI, so I would anchor the answer in that actual pipeline.
38 How would you handle Azure OpenAI throttling

I would inspect throttling responses and quota signals, control concurrency, and smooth bursts before the model call. Retry handling would respect the returned retry delay when available and use bounded backoff with jitter otherwise. I would account for existing SDK retries so retries do not multiply across layers. Quota varies by region, model, and deployment type; the context window is a separate limit. I would monitor throttling and queue delay and return a clear overload response if the task deadline cannot be met. [S6]
39 How do you keep an agent from running forever

I would enforce maximum run duration, model calls, tool calls, and token or cost allowances in the orchestrator. Progress would be persisted so a worker restart does not blindly repeat side effects. The run state would record completed steps and cancellation requests. Before each expensive or sensitive step, I would check remaining allowance and authorization. When a limit is reached, the system should stop safely and explain the outcome. A prompt requesting brevity does not provide a reliable operational limit.
40 How would you release a model or prompt change

I would version model deployment, prompt, tools, retrieval configuration, and evaluation data. Before production, I would run representative and adversarial cases, including failure and permission tests. I would compare quality, latency, tool-call behavior, and cost per completed task against the baseline. A staged rollout would allow reversal to a known-good configuration. Live monitoring should detect quality drift and changes in user traffic. I would agree on acceptable tradeoffs with AI and product engineers rather than treat a prompt edit as a risk-free text change.

Understand agent orchestration choices: fixed sequence for predictable stages, controlled parallelism for independent work, and handoff only when routing adds value. More agents add state, coordination, quota, and debugging overhead. [S7]
Design a secure document analysis agent on Azure

Practice prompt: enterprise users upload documents and ask an agent to extract information, retrieve relevant evidence, and produce a report. Some jobs take minutes. Explain your design in 20 minutes and reserve five minutes for tradeoffs.
A strong opening

I would first ask about peak users, document size, job duration, tenant isolation, retention, required accuracy, expected completion time, and recovery objectives. I would distinguish an interactive answer from an asynchronous report. I would also confirm where data and model processing are permitted before choosing regions or deployments.

User -> API Management -> Run API -> Durable run database
Run API -> Outbox dispatcher -> Queue -> Agent workers
Workers -> Document storage / Retrieval / Model / Approved tools
All stages -> Correlated telemetry and per-run usage ledger
Explain the flow

1. Authenticate the user, authorize the tenant, and validate file and request limits. Accept a run with an idempotency key. Persist run state and dispatch intent atomically.
2. Validate uploads, ingest documents, and build permission-aware retrieval. Workers process durable jobs with bounded concurrency.
3. Each agent step checks authorization and allowance, calls the model or tool with a deadline, and records progress.
4. Save the result and completion state; provide status polling or controlled streaming. Retries must not duplicate external actions.
Add the operational design

Use workload identities, restricted storage access, and Key Vault for unavoidable secrets. Define maximum run duration and tool-call limits. Scale workers against queue age and downstream capacity. Monitor completed-task rate, queue age, tail latency, dependency failures, and estimated cost. Keep tenant authorization in retrieval and cache keys. Release immutable artifacts and versioned agent configuration; test recovery, backup restoration, and incompatible data changes.
State your tradeoffs

I would start with managed container hosting unless Kubernetes control is required. I would use a queue for long work, accepting eventual completion in return for resilience and load smoothing. A second region adds cost and data complexity, so its need follows recovery objectives. Retrieval quality and model selection are evaluation decisions. I would explain the smallest useful architecture first, then show how it grows.
Self-check: Did you explain failure handling, tenant boundaries, idempotency, persistent state, quota, cost, monitoring, and release recovery? Avoid drawing every Azure service you know.
41 Errors jump immediately after a release

I would stop further rollout, compare the new and old versions, and inspect user impact, traces, readiness, and recent configuration or schema changes. If the previous version is compatible with current data, I would roll back or route traffic back. I would verify recovery using successful user journeys and monitor delayed jobs. If rollback is unsafe because data changed, I would consider disabling the feature or applying a compatible forward fix. After restoration, I would reproduce the issue and improve the release checks. [S1]
Follow-up: What if the database migration removed a column? Explain why application rollback alone may fail.
42 Agent latency triples while CPU remains low

Low CPU does not rule out saturation. I would split end-to-end latency into queue wait, retrieval, database, model, and tool spans. I would compare prompt size, output length, retry count, connection pool wait, and model throttling before and after the change. If a dependency is limiting throughput, I would control concurrency or route only to a validated alternative. I would avoid simply increasing replicas, which may add pressure to the same bottleneck.
43 Queue age rises although workers are scaling

I would compare arrival rate with successful completion rate and inspect worker failures, processing duration, retry volume, and dead letters. More replicas cannot solve poison messages, database contention, or model quota saturation. I would isolate bad work, set retry limits, and check acknowledgement or lock handling. I would validate a concurrency setting that improves actual completions. During recovery, I would preserve tenant fairness and communicate expected delay rather than allow an uncontrolled drain that overwhelms downstream services.
44 A workload loses access to Key Vault

I would identify the error class first: authentication, authorization, DNS, networking, or service availability. I would check the workload identity binding, token audience, assigned permissions, resource scope, and recent changes. For private access, I would verify DNS resolution and network rules from the workload environment. A safe mitigation might restore a prior valid configuration. I would not make the vault public or grant broad administrator access to hide the issue. After recovery, I would add a check for the actual access path.

Answer order for any incident: impact -> recent change -> evidence -> safe mitigation -> verify recovery -> permanent improvement. Be ready to state what additional evidence would distinguish two plausible causes.
45 How do you show ownership

I see ownership as following a change through deployment and ongoing operation. My CV includes release automation, production on-call work, RCA, and improvements to alerts and runbooks. I would choose a real example where I helped restore service and then completed prevention work rather than stopping when the alert cleared. I would explain what I personally did, how I involved the right people, and what the follow-up changed. The example should show reliable follow-through rather than imply I solved everything alone.
46 Tell me about disagreement with another engineer

Use a real situation rather than memorize a fictional conflict. A useful structure is: we had different views on a deployment or architecture choice; I clarified the constraints and failure risks; we compared a small experiment or production evidence; we documented the decision and responsibilities. Explain where you changed your own view if that happened. The outcome can be a better decision and working relationship, even when your original suggestion was not selected.
47 How do you balance deadline cost and reliability

I would separate essential service protections from improvements that can follow. Identity, recoverable releases, and visibility into production failures are difficult to defer safely. I would simplify the feature or architecture to meet the deadline, make the remaining risks explicit, and give the owner a clear choice with consequences. I would track temporary exceptions with owners and review dates. Cost decisions would preserve the agreed user outcome and service objective instead of reducing capacity without checking impact.
48 Why do you want this job and what are your logistics

I am interested in the combination of AI platform engineering and operational responsibility. It matches my backend, Azure, deployment, and production support experience while giving me room to deepen cost governance. For logistics, I would state my actual notice period, Abu Dhabi commute or relocation position, work authorization, and compensation expectations. I would not invent availability. I would also clarify how the permanent full-time employment description relates to the initial three-to-six-month project duration.
Questions to ask the interviewer

What is running today, and which reliability problem matters most? Who owns on-call, platform security, and cost approvals? What are the current model deployments, request volumes, and quotas? How are agent quality and successful tasks measured? What should this hire deliver in the first 90 days? How will employment and assignment continuation work after the initial project period?
Prepare one real mistake and learning story, one teamwork story, and one documentation example. Keep the focus on your actions and results, and avoid blaming previous colleagues.
These are design exercises for practice. Implement them locally if time allows; the outlines below are not complete production code.
Exercise 1 Implement a run API in Python or TypeScript

Build POST /runs and GET /runs/{id}. Accept an idempotency key, return 202 for accepted work, and persist state. Answer checklist: validated schema; tenant from verified identity; authorization on status reads; unique tenant/key constraint; request-hash conflict handling; durable dispatch intent; consistent error responses. Test a duplicate request, a conflicting request, cross-tenant access, and a crash between transaction commit and publication.
Exercise 2 Write bounded retry pseudocode

for each allowed attempt:
  enforce the overall deadline
  call dependency with a per-attempt timeout
  if success: return result
  if non-transient or unsafe to repeat: fail
  wait using server retry delay or backoff with jitter
  stop if delay exceeds the remaining deadline
fail with a classified error

Explain: retry only appropriate failures; account for SDK retries; prevent duplicate side effects with idempotency; stop on cancellation; log attempt count and final outcome. A retry policy must not turn a short user deadline into an unlimited background operation. [S8]
Exercise 3 Diagnose a deployment from evidence

Practice evidence: old pods are ready; new pods report missing configuration; the rollout has stalled; the database schema is unchanged. Expected response: stop rollout, preserve logs, restore the valid configuration or previous version, verify readiness and business behavior, then add startup configuration validation and a pipeline smoke test. Discuss how your decision changes if schema changes are incompatible.
Exercise 4 Estimate cost and capacity

Given 12,000 tasks/day, two model calls per task, and a hypothetical USD 0.006 per call, model cost is USD 144/day and USD 4,320 for a 30-day month before retries and other services. If 10% of calls repeat, model cost becomes USD 158.40/day. For capacity, 60 tasks/minute with a mean 10-second active duration implies roughly 10 concurrent tasks under stable-flow assumptions. Peak bursts, multiple calls per task, tail latency, and downstream quotas need separate headroom.
Ask yourself: What assumptions drive each result? Which metric validates them? Why might average capacity be insufficient? How would you enforce tenant fairness and avoid an unbounded queue?

pages.title: Seven Day Study Plan and Mock Interview

blocks.text: A practical daily plan

Day 1: rehearse your introduction and two project stories. Verify dates, ownership, and CV metrics. Draw the current platform from memory.
Day 2: Azure architecture, environment boundaries, identities, networking, and recovery. Practice the whiteboard design aloud.
Day 3: APIs, idempotency, queues, database consistency, and Python or Node concurrency. Complete the run-API exercise.
Day 4: CI/CD, Terraform or Bicep, containers, probes, scaling, and rollback. Explain one actual pipeline in detail.
Day 5: telemetry and incidents. Work through all four troubleshooting scenarios and prepare a real RCA story.
Day 6: cloud and LLM cost, quotas, RAG operations, and security. Repeat the cost calculation without notes.
Day 7: run a timed mock interview, review weak answers, and prepare recruiter logistics and your questions.
If the interview is within 24 hours

Spend 30 minutes on the introduction and project evidence; 45 on Azure design and identities; 45 on CI/CD and Kubernetes; 45 on incidents and observability; 45 on cost, quotas, and agent limits; and 30 on a timed mock and recruiter questions. Take short breaks. Prioritize explanations you can defend over memorizing tool lists.
A 60 minute mock interview

Minutes 0-5: introduction and role fit. 5-15: one project and technical follow-ups. 15-30: Azure system design. 30-40: deployment and production incident. 40-48: cost and AI security. 48-55: behavior and logistics. 55-60: your questions. Have the interviewer ask why, what failed, and what you would change after each main answer.
Score each answer from zero to two

Give yourself up to two points each for directness, technical correctness, personal evidence, tradeoffs, and operational detail. A strong answer scores at least eight of ten and survives a follow-up. Record weak areas and repeat only those. For design questions, personal evidence can be a relevant prior lesson rather than a claim that you implemented the proposed design.
Final rehearsal checklist

Can I explain my two best projects without the CV? Can I distinguish message reliability from service availability? Can I explain a safe rollback and an unsafe one? Can I diagnose throttling without adding replicas? Can I calculate token cost and state the assumptions? Can I explain tenant authorization and agent tool boundaries? Can I discuss the gaps honestly and give a credible learning plan?
Remember these distinctions

Budget alert: spending notification; application quota: runtime enforcement. Readiness: receive traffic; liveness: restart decision; startup: protect initialization. HPA: pod count; cluster autoscaler: node capacity. Authentication: who you are; authorization: what you may do. RTO: time to restore; RPO: acceptable data loss. Retry: repeat an attempt; idempotency: protect against repeated effects. SLI: measurement; SLO: target; SLA: service agreement. Throughput, availability, and test coverage are separate measures.
